claim: Network contractions are driven by the clustering of microtubule minus ends by dynein.
source: We propose that these contractions are driven by the clustering of microtubule minus ends by dynein.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on experimental observations and theoretical modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: The timescale of contraction depends on initial network geometry.
source: Based on this idea, we construct an active fluid theory of network contractions, which predicts a dependence of the timescale of contraction on initial network geometry, a development of density inhomogeneities during contraction, a constant final network density, and a strong influence of dynein inhibition on the rate of contraction, all in quantitative agreement with experiments.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing different contraction timescales for different channel widths (Figure 3).

claim: Density inhomogeneities develop during contraction.
source: Based on this idea, we construct an active fluid theory of network contractions, which predicts a dependence of the timescale of contraction on initial network geometry, a development of density inhomogeneities during contraction, a constant final network density, and a strong influence of dynein inhibition on the rate of contraction, all in quantitative agreement with experiments.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements of density profiles showing increased density at network edges (Figure 5).

claim: Networks contract to a constant final density independent of initial conditions.
source: Based on this idea, we construct an active fluid theory of network contractions, which predicts a dependence of the timescale of contraction on initial network geometry, a development of density inhomogeneities during contraction, a constant final network density, and a strong influence of dynein inhibition on the rate of contraction, all in quantitative agreement with experiments.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing constant ε∞ across different channel geometries (Figure 3F).

claim: Dynein inhibition strongly influences the rate of contraction.
source: Based on this idea, we construct an active fluid theory of network contractions, which predicts a dependence of the timescale of contraction on initial network geometry, a development of density inhomogeneities during contraction, a constant final network density, and a strong influence of dynein inhibition on the rate of contraction, all in quantitative agreement with experiments.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing dose-dependent slowdown of contraction with p150-CC1 (Figure 6).

claim: Motor-driven clustering of filament ends is a generic mechanism leading to contraction.
source: These results demonstrate that the motor-driven clustering of filament ends is a generic mechanism leading to contraction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental and theoretical results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Motor proteins including dynein and roughly 14 different families of kinesin organize microtubules to form the spindle.
source: Motor proteins, including dynein and roughly 14 different families of kinesin (Wordeman, 2010), organize microtubules to form the spindle, which segregates chromosomes during cell division.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Myosin organizes actin filaments into networks which drive cell motility, polarity, cytokinesis, and left-right symmetry breakage.
source: The motor protein myosin organizes actin filaments into networks which drive cell motility, polarity, cytokinesis, and left-right symmetry breakage (Mitchinson and Cramer, 1996; Mayer et al., 2010; Naganathan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Actin can form macroscopic networks that exhibit myosin-dependent bulk contraction.
source: Actin can form macroscopic networks that exhibit a myosin-dependent bulk contraction (Murrell and Gardel, 2012; Bendix et al., 2008; Köhler and Bausch, 2012; Alvarado et al., 2013; Szent-Györgyi, 1943).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Microtubule networks purified from neuronal extracts undergo bulk contraction.
source: Microtubule networks purified from neuronal extracts have also been observed to undergo bulk contraction (Weisenberg and Cianci, 1984)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Microtubules in mitotic and meiotic extracts assemble into asters.
source: while microtubules in mitotic and meiotic extracts are found to assemble into asters (Gaglio et al., 1995; Mountain et al., 1999; Verde et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Aster formation in meiotic Xenopus egg extracts is dynein-dependent.
source: Aster formation in meiotic Xenopus egg extracts is dynein-dependent, and has been proposed to be driven by the clustering of microtubule minus ends by dynein (Verde et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Dynein binds to the minus ends of microtubules in spindles and clusters the minus ends to form spindle poles.
source: It has also been suggested that dynein binds to the minus ends of microtubules in spindles and clusters the minus ends of microtubules to form spindle poles (Heald et al., 1996; Burbank et al., 2007; Khodjakov et al., 2003; Goshima et al., 2005; Elting et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Dynein accumulates on microtubule minus ends in a purified system.
source: and dynein has been shown to accumulate on microtubule minus ends in a purified system (McKenney et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Purified solutions of microtubules and kinesin can form asters.
source: Purified solutions of microtubules and kinesin can also form asters (Nédélec et al., 1997; Hentrich and Surrey, 2010; Urrutia et al., 1991)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Purified solutions of microtubules and kinesin can form dynamic liquid crystalline networks under certain conditions.
source: or under other conditions, dynamic liquid crystalline networks (Sanchez et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Hydrodynamic theories describe the behaviors of cytoskeletal networks on length scales much greater than individual filaments and motor proteins.
source: Hydrodynamic theories have been proposed to describe the behaviors of cytoskeletal networks on length scales that are much greater than the size of individual filaments and motor proteins (Prost et al., 2015, Marchetti et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Contractile stresses can result from a preferred association of motors with filament ends.
source: Contractile stresses can result from a preferred association of motors with filament ends (Kruse and Jülicher, 2000; Hyman and Karsenti, 1996)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Contractile stresses can result from nonlinear elasticity of the network.
source: nonlinear elasticity of the network (Liverpool et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Contractile stresses can result from the buckling of individual filaments.
source: or the buckling of individual filaments (Murrell and Gardel, 2012; Lenz, 2014; Soares e Silva et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Extensile active stresses can arise from polarity sorting or from the mechanical properties of individual molecular motors.
source: Extensile active stresses can arise from polarity sorting or result from the mechanical properties of individual molecular motors (Gao et al., 2015; Blackwell et al. 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Acto-myosin systems are observed to be contractile.
source: Experimentally, acto-myosin systems (Murrell and Gardel, 2012; Bendix et al., 2008; Köhler and Bausch, 2012; Alvarado et al., 2013; Szent-Györgyi, 1943) and microtubule networks from neuronal extracts (Weisenberg and Cianci, 1984) are observed to be contractile
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Purified solutions of microtubules and kinesin can form extensile liquid crystalline networks.
source: while purified solutions of microtubules and kinesin can form extensile liquid crystalline networks (Sanchez et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Xenopus egg extracts recapitulate a range of cell biological processes, including spindle assembly and chromosome segregation.
source: These extracts are nearly undiluted cytoplasm and recapitulate a range of cell biological processes, including spindle assembly and chromosome segregation (Hannak and Heald, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Taxol causes microtubules to rapidly assemble and stabilize.
source: Taxol causes microtubules to rapidly assemble and stabilize (Mitchison et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Microtubules organized into asters in some regions of the channel.
source: In some regions of the channel, microtubules organized into asters (Figure 1B) as observed previously (Verde et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1B and cited prior work.

claim: NUMA antibody localizes to microtubule minus ends.
source: A NUMA antibody was used to locate microtubule minus ends (Mitchison et al., 2013), and was found to localize to the aster core, confirming the polarity of the aster (Gaglio et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and citations to prior literature.

claim: Isolated asters interact and coalesce.
source: Isolated asters were found to interact and coalesce (Figure 1C, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1C and Video 1.

claim: Microtubules formed networks of aster-like structures in other regions of the channel.
source: In other regions of the channel, microtubules formed networks of aster-like structures (Figure 1D)
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Aster-like structures are highly dynamic and exhibit large-scale motion that persists for several tens of seconds.
source: which were highly dynamic and exhibited large-scale motion that persisted for several tens of seconds (Figure 1E, Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1E and Video 2.

claim: NUMA localizes to the interior of aster-like structures.
source: NUMA was found to localize to the interior of these structures, confirming their aster-like nature (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figures 1F and 1G.

claim: The contractile behavior of microtubule networks is reminiscent of actin network contractions in these extracts.
source: The contractile behavior of these microtubule networks is highly reminiscent of the contractions of actin networks in these extracts (Bendix et al., 2008)
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work supported by citation.

claim: Network tears have little impact on contraction dynamics far from the tearing site.
source: Occasionally, we observed networks tearing along their length (Video 4), yet these tears seemed to have little impact on the contraction dynamics far from the tearing site
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Video 4.

claim: Networks in smaller channels contract faster.
source: Visual inspection of the fraction-contracted curves, ϵ(t), reveals that networks in smaller channels contract faster
evidence: This is observed from experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: All networks reach a similar final fraction contracted regardless of channel width.
source: but all reach a similar final fraction contracted (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The dependence of τ on channel width is inconsistent with viscoelastic or poroelastic timescales.
source: We find that the dependence of τ on channel width is inconsistent with the time of contraction resulting from either viscoelastic or poroelastic timescales, which would predict constant and quadratic scalings respectively (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and comparison to theoretical predictions.

claim: τ does not significantly vary with channel height.
source: We next explored the influence of channel height H0 (H0 = 75, 125, 150 μm, all with width W0 = 1.4 mm) and found that τ does not significantly vary in these channels (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: All networks contracted to the same final density since Taxol concentration was held constant.
source: Since the Taxol concentration was held constant, all experiments started with the same initial density of microtubules, regardless of the dimensions of the channel. Thus, all networks contracted to the same final density.
evidence: This is inferred from the constant ε∞ and constant initial conditions.

claim: Drag could arise from weak interactions between the microtubule network and the device wall.
source: and thus could arise from weak interactions between the microtubule network and the device wall.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that drag is independent of channel height.

claim: Contracting networks consist of microtubule asters.
source: As the contracting networks consist of microtubule asters (Figure 1D, E)
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: Microtubule asters in meiotic extracts assemble by dynein-induced clustering of microtubule minus ends.
source: and microtubule asters in meiotic extracts are thought to assemble by the dynein-induced clustering of microtubule minus ends (Verde et al., 1991)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The contraction process is driven by dynein pulling microtubule minus ends towards each other.
source: we hypothesize that the contraction process is also driven by dynein pulling microtubule minus ends towards each other (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on prior work and experimental observations, illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: Steric collisions counteract the contractile stress at high densities.
source: As only a finite number of microtubules can fit near the core of an aster, steric collisions will counteract the contractile stress at high densities (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a theoretical consideration illustrated in Figure 4B.

claim: The predicted scaling of τ with W₀ is consistent with experimental data and simulations.
source: This predicted scaling is both consistent with the experimental data and simulations of the full theory (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of theoretical predictions to experimental data and simulations shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The microtubule density increases at the network's edge during contraction.
source: To test this, we averaged the fluorescence intensity along the length of the channel (see Materials and Methods) and found that the microtubule density does indeed increase at the network's edge during contraction (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The inhomogeneous density profile is quantitatively explained by the active fluid theory.
source: We next explored if the inhomogeneous density profile could be quantitatively explained by our active fluid theory. We numerically solved Equations (3,4,5) and used least squares fitting to determine the simulation parameters which most closely matched the experimentally measured profiles (Figure 5B)
evidence: This is supported by comparison of simulations to experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Fitting simulations to density profiles yields η/(sρ₀²) = 0.82 ± 0.03 min, γ/(sρ₀²) = 6.1 ± 0.1×10⁻⁶ min/(μm²), and ρᵢₙᵢₜᵢₐₗ/ρ₀ = 0.32 ± 0.01.
source: yielding η∕(sρ02) = 0.82 ± 0.03 min, γ∕(sρ02) = 6.1 ± 0.1×10-6 min/(μm2), and ρinitial∕ρ0 = 0.32  ±  0.01 (mean  ±  s.e.m., n=4 experiments).
evidence: This is obtained by fitting simulations to experimental density profiles.

claim: The fitted parameter values from density profiles are the same as those determined from the dependence of τ on channel width.
source: Within error, these values are the same as those determined from the dependence of the timescale of contraction on channel width (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a comparison of parameter values obtained from two different experimental approaches.

claim: Simulated profiles closely match experimental ones for most of the contraction.
source: The simulated profiles closely match the experimental ones for most of the contraction (Figure 5B)
evidence: This is supported by visual comparison of simulations and experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: At late times, simulated inhomogeneities dissipate in contrast to experiments.
source: but at late times the simulated inhomogeneities dissipate in contrast to the experiments (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from comparison of simulations and experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The discrepancy at late times might be caused by long-term aging of the network not incorporated into the model.
source: This might be caused by a long-term aging of the network that is not incorporated into our simple model.
evidence: This is a speculation about the cause of the discrepancy between simulations and experiments.

claim: Velocities increase superlinearly with distance from the network's center.
source: To confirm that the density buildup was due to an increased velocity near the network's edge, we measured the velocity throughout the network using Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV, see Materials and Methods) (Figure 5C) and found that the velocities increase superlinearly with distance from the network's center, as predicted (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by PIV measurements shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: Aster assembly is dynein-dependent in Xenopus egg extracts.
source: Aster assembly is dynein-dependent in Xenopus egg extracts (Gaglio et al.,1995; Verde et al., 1991)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Dynein and Kinesin-5 are two of the most dominant motors in spindle assembly in Xenopus egg extracts.
source: and dynein (Heald et al., 1996) and Kinesin-5 (Sawin et al., 1992) are two of the most dominant motors in spindle assembly in this system.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Inhibiting Kinesin-5 had little effect on the contraction process.
source: Inhibiting Kinesin-5 had little effect on the contraction process (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inhibiting dynein caused a dose-dependent slowdown of the contraction.
source: In contrast, inhibiting dynein caused a dose-dependent slowdown of the contraction (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In spindle assembly, inhibiting Kinesin-5 suppresses the morphological changes caused by dynein inhibition.
source: In spindle assembly, inhibiting Kinesin-5 suppresses the morphological changes caused by dynein inhibition (Mitchison et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The effects of dynein inhibition were not rescued by simultaneous inhibition of Kinesin-5.
source: We, therefore, tested how simultaneously inhibiting both motors influences the contraction process, but found that the effects of dynein inhibition were not rescued by the simultaneous inhibition of Kinesin-5 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In this context, Kinesin-5 is not generating a counteracting extensile stress.
source: suggesting that in this context, Kinesin-5 is not generating a counteracting extensile stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that simultaneous inhibition of Kinesin-5 does not rescue dynein inhibition effects.

claim: In the spindle, the role of Kinesin-5 may be in orienting, polarity sorting, and sliding microtubules as opposed to active stress generation.
source: This further suggests the possibility that in the spindle, the role of Kinesin-5 may be in orienting, polarity sorting, and sliding microtubules as opposed to active stress generation.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental observations.

claim: The characteristic time τ can be tuned over a wide range from approximately 3 min to approximately 75 min by varying p150-CC1 concentration.
source: By varying the concentration of p150-CC1, the characteristic time, τ, could be tuned over a wide range from ≈ 3 min to ≈ 75 min (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The EC50 value for p150-CC1 effect on contraction timescale is 0.22 ± 0.02 μM.
source: Fitting a sigmoid function to the τ vs. p150-CC1 concentration curve yields an EC50 value of 0.22  ± . 02 μM (mean  ±  standard error)
evidence: This is obtained by fitting a sigmoid function to experimental data.

claim: The EC50 value is similar to the value of approximately 0.3 μM reported for the effect of p150-CC1 on spindle length in Xenopus extracts.
source: similar to the value of ≈ 0.3 μM reported for the effect of p150-CC1 on spindle length in Xenopus extracts (Gaetz and Kapoor, 2004)
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work supported by citation.

claim: The similarity in EC50 values is consistent with active stress generated by dynein being required for pole focusing.
source: which is consistent with active stress generated by dynein being required for pole focusing.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the similarity of EC50 values.

claim: There are no apparent differences in ε∞ despite large changes in contraction timescale with p150-CC1 concentration.
source: Despite this large change in the contraction timescale, we found no apparent differences in ϵ∞ (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Microtubule networks contract to approximately the same final density irrespective of p150-CC1 concentration.
source: Thus, the microtubule networks contract to approximately the same final density irrespective of the concentration of p150-CC1.
evidence: This is inferred from the constant ε∞ across different p150-CC1 concentrations.

claim: The observation that inhibiting dynein affects the timescale but not the final density is consistent with model predictions.
source: The observation that inhibiting dynein affects the timescale of contraction but not the final density to which the network contracts is consistent with the predictions of our model.
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental observations to theoretical predictions.

claim: Even at the highest p150-CC1 concentrations, the network still undergoes bulk contraction.
source: We note that even at the highest p150-CC1 concentrations used, the network still undergoes a bulk contraction.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data.

claim: Residual contraction at high p150-CC1 could be due to incomplete inhibition of dynein or another motor protein.
source: This could possibly be due to incomplete inhibition of dynein by p150-CC1, or by another motor protein present in the extract that also contributes to the contraction process.
evidence: This is a speculation about the cause of residual contraction.

claim: The strength of the active stress in the 2 μM p150-CC1 condition is approximately 4% of the strength in the uninhibited case.
source: As the characteristic time, τ∝1s, by comparing the characteristic times in the uninhibited and 2 μM p150-CC1 cases, we can estimate that the strength of the active stress, s, in the 2 μM p150-CC1 condition is only ≈ 4% of the strength of the active stress in the uninhibited case
evidence: This is estimated by comparing characteristic times under different conditions.

claim: Even if another motor is involved in contraction, dynein contributes approximately 96% of the active stress.
source: arguing that even if another motor is involved in the contraction, dynein contributes ≈ 96% of the active stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the estimate that the active stress at high p150-CC1 is 4% of the uninhibited case.

claim: Networks of stabilized microtubules in Xenopus egg extracts undergo bulk contraction.
source: Here, we have shown that networks of stabilized microtubules in Xenopus egg extracts undergo a bulk contraction.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental finding.

claim: The timescale of contraction is not a poroelastic or viscoelastic timescale.
source: By systematically varying the width of the microfluidic channel in which the network forms, we demonstrated that the timescale of contraction is not a poroelastic or viscoelastic timescale.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data showing the dependence of τ on channel width.

claim: A simple active fluid model correctly predicts multiple features of network contraction.
source: A simple active fluid model of network contraction by dynein-driven clustering of microtubule minus ends correctly predicts the dependence of the contraction timescale on channel width, the nonuniform density profile in the network during contraction, and that inhibiting dynein affects the timescale of contraction but not the final density that the network contracts to.
evidence: This is a summary of the agreement between theoretical predictions and experimental observations.

claim: Model parameters can be measured by the scaling of contraction timescale with channel width and by analysis of network inhomogeneities.
source: Parameters of this model can be measured by the scaling of the contraction timescale with channel width and by a detailed analysis of the inhomogeneities in the network that develop during contraction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the two independent methods used to determine model parameters.

claim: Both methods for measuring model parameters give similar values.
source: Both methods give similar values.
evidence: This is stated as a result of comparing parameter values obtained from two different approaches.

claim: The behaviors of a complex biological system can be quantitatively described by a simple active matter continuum theory.
source: Our results demonstrate that the behaviors of a complex biological system can be quantitatively described by a simple active matter continuum theory.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the agreement between theory and experiments.

claim: Active matter theories aim to describe cytoskeletal systems at large-length scales and long-timescales by averaging molecular complexity into coarse-grained parameters.
source: These active matter theories aim to describe the behavior of cytoskeletal systems at large-length scales and long-timescales by effectively averaging all of the molecular complexity into a small set of coarse-grained parameters.
evidence: This is a description of the approach used in active matter theories.

claim: Previously, active matter theories have been predominantly applied to describe biological systems near non-equilibrium steady states.
source: Previously, these theories have been predominately applied to describe biological systems near non-equilibrium steady states (Prost et al., 2015; Brugués et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The present work augments previous theories with a nonlinear active stress term to capture far from steady state dynamics.
source: In the present work, we augment previous theories with a nonlinear active stress term derived from microscopic considerations to capture the far from steady state dynamics of the contraction process.
evidence: This describes the novel contribution of the present work.

claim: The approach allows quantitative explanation of experimental results using a theory with only four parameters.
source: This approach allows us to quantitatively explain our experimental results using a theory with only four parameters
evidence: This is a statement about the simplicity and effectiveness of the theoretical approach.

claim: A complete microscopic model would require understanding the behavior of thousands of different proteins in Xenopus egg extracts.
source: while a complete microscopic model would require understanding the behavior of the thousands of different proteins present in Xenopus egg extracts.
evidence: This is a statement about the complexity of the biological system.

claim: The considerations of the model are general.
source: Furthermore, the considerations of the model are general
evidence: This is a statement about the generalizability of the model.

claim: The end clustering mechanism could contribute to contraction in actin networks as well.
source: and it will be interesting to consider whether the end clustering mechanism proposed here could contribute to contraction in actin networks as well.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential applicability of the mechanism to other systems.

claim: The active stress which drives network contraction results from motor-induced clustering of microtubule minus ends.
source: In our model, the active stress which drives network contraction results from the motor-induced clustering of microtubule minus ends
evidence: This is a statement of the key mechanism in the model.

claim: Minus end clustering is the same process thought to be responsible for aster formation and spindle pole focusing.
source: the same process thought to be responsible for aster formation and spindle pole focusing (Gaglio et al., 1995; Mountain et al., 1999; Verde et al., 1991, Elting et al., 2014; Heald et al., 1996; Burbank et al., 2007; Khodjakov et al., 2003; Goshima et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Results and previous data are consistent with minus end clustering in Xenopus egg extracts primarily arising from dynein activity.
source: Our results, and previous data (Verde et al., 1991; Heald et al., 1996; Burbank et al., 2007), are consistent with minus end clustering in Xenopus egg extracts primarily arising from the activity of dynein.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to prior literature.

claim: Dynein's ability to cluster minus ends could result from accumulating on one microtubule minus end while walking towards the minus end of another.
source: The ability of dynein to cluster microtubule minus ends could result from dynein being able to accumulate on the minus end of one microtubule, while simultaneously walking towards the minus end of another (Hyman and Karsenti, 1996; McKenney et al. 2014; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: There is indication that such dynein behaviors may occur in spindles.
source: There is indication that such behaviors may indeed occur in spindles (Elting et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Microtubule networks contracting in Xenopus egg extracts suggests that motor-induced stresses in spindles are net contractile.
source: The observation that microtubule networks contract in Xenopus egg extracts suggests that motor-induced stresses in spindles are net contractile and not extensile as previously assumed (Brugués and Needleman, 2014).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Dynein's contribution to spindle pole focusing may be due to contractile stresses.
source: The contribution of dynein to spindle pole focusing may ultimately be due to these contractile stresses.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Contractile stresses from dynein might explain that spindle fusion is dynein-dependent.
source: The presence of contractile stresses from dynein might also explain both the observation that the fusion of spindles is dynein-dependent (Gatlin et al., 2009)
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Contractile stresses from dynein might explain the greater cohesion between microtubules at spindle poles.
source: and the apparently greater cohesion between microtubules at spindle poles, (where dynein is localized [Gatlin et al., 2010]).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citation to prior work.

claim: It is unclear what processes set the density of microtubules in the spindle.
source: It is unclear what processes set the density of microtubules in the spindle
evidence: This is a statement about current knowledge gaps.

claim: The active stress from minus end clustering saturating at a preferred microtubule density could play an important role in setting spindle microtubule density.
source: and the finding that the active stress generated from minus end clustering saturates at a preferred microtubule density could play an important role.
evidence: This is a speculation about the implications of the findings.

claim: CSF-arrested extracts were prepared from Xenopus laevis oocytes.
source: CSF-arrested extracts were prepared from Xenopus llaevis oocytes as previously described (Hannak and Heald, 2006).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Crude extracts were sequentially filtered through 2.0, 1.2, and 0.2 micron filters.
source: Crude extracts were sequentially filtered through 2.0, 1.2, and 0.2 micron filters, frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at −80°C until use.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Microfluidic devices were fabricated using PDMS cast onto masters made from tape channel negatives.
source: Channel negatives were designed using AutoCAD 360 (Autodesk) and Silhouette Studio (Silhouette America) software, cut from 125-micron-thick tape (3M Scotchcal, St. Paul, MN) using a Silhouette Cameo die cutter, and a master was made by adhering channel negatives to the bottom of a petri dish. PDMS (Sylgard 184, Dow Corning, Midland, MI; 10:1 mixing ratio) was cast onto the masters and cured overnight at 60°C.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Channels were treated with BSA and Pluronic F127 before use.
source: Channels containing a degassed solution of 5 mg/mL BSA (J.T. Baker, Center Valley, PA) supplemented with 2.5% w/w Pluronic F127 (Sigma, St. Louis, MO) were incubated overnight at 12°C.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: GST-tagged p150-CC1 was expressed in E. coli and purified using a GSTrap column.
source: GST-p150-CC1 was expressed in E. coli BL21 (DE3)-T1R(Sigma) for 4 hr at 37°C. The culture was shifted to 18°C for 1 hr before adding 0.2 mM IPTG and the culture was grown overnight at 18°C. Cells were centrifuged, resuspended in PBS supplemented with Halt Protease Inhibitor Cocktail (Thermo Scientific, Rockford, IL) and benzonase (Novagen, San Diego, CA) before lysis by sonication. GST-p150-CC1 was purified from clarified lysate using a GSTrap column FF (G.E. Healthcare, Sweden) as per the manufacturer's instructions.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Images were acquired using a spinning disk confocal microscope with a 2x objective.
source: Channels were sealed with vacuum grease and imaged using a spinning disk confocal microscope (Nikon Ti2000, Yokugawa CSU-X1), an EMCCD camera (Hamamatsu), and a 2x objective using Metamorph acquisition software (Molecular Devices).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Particle Imaging Velocimetry was performed using PIVLab software.
source: Particle Imaging Velocimetry was performed using PIVLab software (Thielicke and Stamhuis, 2014) using the FFT window deformation algorithm with a 16-pixel interrogation area and 8 pixel step for the first pass and an 8 pixel interrogation area with a 4-pixel step for the second pass.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods.
